constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Data-driven advocacy for certified school librarian staffing
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: As school librarian at Valley View K-8, craft a constructive, evidence-driven advocacy strategy to demonstrate the instructional and equity impact of a full-time certified librarian ahead of a district staffing reduction proposal.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Facing a district shortfall, the superintendent proposes cutting Valley View K-8’s full-time certified school librarian to 0.5 FTE and staffing the library with an untrained clerk three days weekly. Program logs document 62 co-taught inquiry lessons across 14 teachers, a 31% gain in scholarly database use by grades 6–8 writers, and 440 after-school digital-access visits by students without home broadband.
taskParts: A. Synthesize the library’s instructional, research, and digital-equity data into a concise executive impact brief aligned to district improvement priorities.
B. Distinguish clearly between clerical circulation duties and the specialized instructional, curation, and accessibility expertise of a certified school librarian.
C. Mobilize faculty, family, and student stakeholders constructively within district governance norms while outlining transparent service-impact projections if staffing drops to 0.5 FTE.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Highlight 62 co-taught lessons across 14 teachers, 31% higher grade 6–8 scholarly database usage, and 440 after-school broadband-access visits tied directly to equity and writing goals.

planningFrame.label: Policy & standards
planningFrame.guidance: Ground advocacy in AASL National School Library Standards on instructional leadership and equitable access, linking certified staffing to district literacy and digital-citizenship targets.

planningFrame.label: Action plan
planningFrame.guidance: Deliver a one-page data brief to the principal and superintendent, invite collaborating teachers and families to share concrete student-learning stories, and map exact instructional losses under a 0.5 FTE clerk model.

planningFrame.label: Accountability & follow-up
planningFrame.guidance: Establish quarterly program-impact reporting tied to school improvement goals so library staffing value remains visible year-round rather than only during budget crises.

successCriteria: Frames advocacy around measurable student learning and digital equity (62 co-taught lessons, 31% database gain, 440 broadband visits) rather than personal job preservation.
Articulates respectfully why a clerk can assist with shelving and checkouts but cannot legally or pedagogically replace certified co-teaching, inquiry assessment, and collection curation.
Works transparently through the building principal and appropriate district governance channels rather than organizing adversarial attacks on administrators.
Includes concrete service-impact modeling showing which co-taught units and after-school access hours would disappear under a 0.5 FTE cut, alongside sustainable year-round reporting.
commonPitfalls: Centering advocacy on circulation totals or personal job security rather than co-taught student learning and closing the 440-visit broadband equity gap.
Disparaging clerical paraprofessionals instead of distinguishing complementary clerical versus certified instructional responsibilities.
Bypassing the principal or attacking the superintendent publicly, which erodes leadership credibility during budget deliberations.
Waiting until a staffing cut is proposed to collect evidence instead of building ongoing quarterly impact reporting aligned to school goals.
sampleOutline: Executive evidence brief: connect the 62 co-taught lessons, 31% grade 6–8 database growth, and 440 after-school broadband visits directly to district literacy and equity priorities.

Role clarity: distinguish clerical operations (shelving, circulation) from certified librarian functions (co-teaching SIFT/inquiry, UDL curation, copyright/privacy stewardship, and formative assessment).

Coalition and governance: partner with the principal first, share transparent 0.5 FTE service-loss scenarios (lost co-teaching blocks and reduced after-school access), and invite teachers, families, and students to contribute student-centered testimonials.
Year-round visibility: institute concise termly library impact dashboards linked to school-improvement metrics to sustain funding long-term.

quickReference.title: AASL Program Vision, Strategic Planning, Budget & Policy
quickReference.purpose: Anchors AASL National School Library Standards, needs assessments, program evaluation, equitable budgeting, and governance policies for Praxis 5312.
checklist: Check how the school library mission, goals, and resource priorities align directly to the school improvement plan and AASL Shared Foundations.
Verify that program budgets, staffing plans, and space updates are backed by needs-assessment data rather than habit or guesswork.
Confirm that board-approved written policies govern material selection, reconsideration, circulation, equipment, and acceptable digital use.
formulas: AASL National School Library Standards Matrix: 6 Shared Foundations (Inquire, Include, Collaborate, Curate, Explore, Engage) intersect with 4 Domains (Think, Create, Share, Grow) across three integrated frameworks—Learner, School Librarian, and School Library.

Program Needs Assessment & Evaluation Cycle: gather quantitative data (circulation trends, collection age/curriculum mapping, database usage, collaborative unit counts) plus qualitative evidence (student inquiry products, teacher/student surveys) to drive annual improvement goals.

Library Budgeting & Funding Models: Line-Item budgets allocate funds by category (print, databases, supplies); Zero-Based budgets justify every cost annually against instructional priorities; supplemental sources include E-rate telecommunications discounts, Title funds, and targeted grants.

Essential Board-Approved Policies: Selection Policy (criteria and review tools), Reconsideration Policy (formal challenge workflow), Circulation & Confidentiality Policy (equitable borrowing and patron privacy), and Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) aligned to district legal counsel.
decisionRules: When taking over a school library with outdated collections and declining teacher use → conduct a comprehensive needs assessment (collection mapping, circulation audit, and teacher/student survey) before drafting a multi-year strategic plan and budget request.

When the principal asks to justify next year’s database subscription renewal during budget cuts → present usage statistics linked to collaborative classroom research units, curriculum standards, and student learning evidence rather than raw seat counts alone.

When a library lacks clear procedures for handling book challenges or damaged-book fines → collaborate with administration and a representative committee to draft board-approved selection, reconsideration, and equitable circulation policies before a crisis occurs.

When managing paraprofessional staff and parent volunteers → establish clear written workflows separating clerical shelving/processing duties from certified librarian responsibilities (instruction, collection selection, and confidential patron data).
cautions: Never run the school library as an isolated warehouse disconnected from schoolwide literacy, inquiry, and equity goals.
Do not allow punitive overdue-fine policies or unpaid-book blocks to bar struggling readers from accessing instructional or choice reading materials when equitable alternatives exist.
Avoid assigning volunteers or student aides access to confidential patron circulation histories or overdue lists.

quickReference.title: Collection Development, CREW/MUSTIE Weeding, Discovery & Privacy
quickReference.purpose: Anchors inclusive curation, selection tools, systematic weeding, cataloging/OPAC organization, flexible scheduling, and patron confidentiality.
checklist: Cross-check collection gaps against curriculum standards, student reading interests, cultural/linguistic diversity, and accessible formats.
Apply objective CREW/MUSTIE criteria and collection-age benchmarks before deselection or replacement.
Verify that cataloging, physical layout, scheduling, and circulation systems maximize equitable discovery while protecting patron privacy.
formulas: CREW Method & MUSTIE Weeding Criteria: Continuous Review, Evaluation, and Weeding removes items that are Misleading (factually inaccurate), Ugly (worn/damaged), Superseded (newer edition/better source), Trivial (no literary/curriculum merit), Irrelevant (no community/curriculum fit), or available Elsewhere (better digital/interlibrary access).

Selection & Diverse Curation Tools: evaluate purchases using professional review journals (School Library Journal, Booklist, Horn Book, Kirkus, VOYA), curriculum mapping, and diversity audits ensuring balanced representation across identities, viewpoints, and languages.

Cataloging & Discovery Standards: MARC21 records, Resource Description and Access (RDA), Dewey Decimal Classification (DDC), and Library of Congress Subject Headings (LCSH) standardize OPAC searchability; thoughtful signage and selective fiction genrefication lower browsing barriers while keeping catalog consistency.

Flexible Scheduling & Patron Confidentiality: Flexible Scheduling grants point-of-need class and individual access for inquiry and co-teaching (superior to rigid Fixed Scheduling tied solely to teacher prep coverage); ALA Library Bill of Rights, FERPA, and state library-privacy statutes bar disclosing a student’s borrowing history to unauthorized parties.
decisionRules: When a collection analysis reveals that the 500s–600s science and health sections average 18 years old → weed outdated or factually misleading titles using CREW/MUSTIE criteria and prioritize current, authoritative print and database replacements.

When a school uses a rigid fixed schedule that treats library time only as teacher planning coverage → advocate for a flexible or modified-flexible schedule by demonstrating how point-of-need co-taught inquiry lifts classroom research outcomes.

When a curious teacher or parent of another student asks what books a specific 7th grader has checked out → decline to disclose the student’s borrowing record under patron-confidentiality ethics and FERPA.

When English learners and students with print disabilities underuse the collection → expand bilingual titles, hi-lo books, audiobooks, digital e-books with adjustable text, and visual OPAC discovery guides.
cautions: Never hoard outdated, tattered, or inaccurate books simply to inflate total book-count-per-student statistics; an outdated shelf hides quality resources and erodes trust.
Do not self-censor or silently discard a controversial but professionally reviewed, curriculum-aligned title just to avoid a possible complaint.
Avoid posting public overdue lists with student names and book titles on bulletin boards or classroom doors, which violates patron privacy.

quickReference.title: Inquiry Models, Lateral Reading, Intellectual Freedom, Fair Use & CIPA
quickReference.purpose: Anchors research/search instruction, source verification, First Amendment intellectual freedom, copyright law, and CIPA compliance.
checklist: Match the inquiry model and search strategy (Boolean logic, databases, lateral reading) to student grade level and research complexity.
Identify the controlling legal rule for information access: formal Reconsideration Policy, 4-factor Fair Use, Creative Commons, or CIPA filtering/unblocking.
Verify that students learn ethical attribution, privacy protection, and critical evaluation rather than merely obeying blocklists.
formulas: Inquiry & Source-Evaluation Frameworks: Stripling Model (Connect, Wonder, Investigate, Construct, Express, Reflect), Big6 (Task Definition through Evaluation), and Guided Inquiry Design scaffold research; Lateral Reading / SIFT (Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to original context) beats surface checklists on web misinformation, paired with Boolean operators (AND narrows, OR broadens, NOT excludes).

Intellectual Freedom & Reconsideration (ALA + Pico): ALA Library Bill of Rights affirms equitable access to diverse ideas; Board of Education, Island Trees v. Pico (1982) restricts removing library books solely to suppress disfavored political or social viewpoints; board-approved Reconsideration Policies require written requests, committee review, and keeping the title accessible until the review concludes.

Copyright & Four-Factor Fair Use (17 U.S.C. Section 107): weigh (1) Purpose and character of use (nonprofit educational and transformative favor fair use), (2) Nature of the copyrighted work (factual favored over creative/consumable), (3) Amount and substantiality used (avoid taking the heart of the work), and (4) Effect on the potential market; Creative Commons (CC BY, NC, SA, ND) clarifies open-reuse permissions.

CIPA (Children’s Internet Protection Act) & Digital Citizenship: schools receiving E-rate discounts must enforce an Internet Safety Policy, run technology protection filters against obscene/harmful content, educate minors on online behavior and cyberbullying, and maintain a prompt procedure for authorized adults to disable/unblock filters for bona fide research.
decisionRules: When a parent verbally demands immediate removal of an award-winning young-adult novel from the shelves → listen respectfully, provide the board-approved Reconsideration Policy and request form, notify administration, and keep the book in circulation while the formal committee reviews it.

When students verify an unfamiliar advocacy website solely by checking its About page and polished design → teach Lateral Reading (SIFT) by opening new tabs to investigate funding, author credibility, and corroboration across reliable journalism and databases.

When a teacher asks the librarian to upload an entire copyrighted textbook PDF to a shared class drive → explain the four Fair Use factors (especially amount copied and market harm), decline full-text copying, and guide the teacher to licensed databases, permissible brief excerpts, or Open Educational Resources (OER).

When an overly restrictive CIPA web filter blocks reputable medical or historical websites needed for an AP research project → follow the district’s CIPA unblocking protocol to request timely review and access for bona fide academic research rather than instructing students to use unauthorized proxy bypasses.
cautions: Never pull a challenged book quietly off the shelf or place it in a secret back room prior to completing the board-approved reconsideration process.

Do not assume every educational classroom use automatically qualifies as Fair Use; copying consumables, entire chapters repeatedly, or showing entertainment movies as pure rewards typically fails the four-factor test.
Avoid teaching students that .org or .edu domains are automatically trustworthy without checking source authority, purpose, and lateral corroboration.

quickReference.title: Collaborative Co-Teaching, UDL Access, Reading Culture & Learning Commons
quickReference.purpose: Anchors instructional partnership, accessible differentiation, reading engagement, media literacy, and purposeful educational technology.
checklist: Confirm that the librarian and classroom teacher co-plan standards, inquiry skills, scaffolds, and rubrics together rather than delivering disconnected library lessons.
Check learning materials and spaces for UDL options, assistive-technology compatibility, and multilingual or sensory accessibility.
Ensure reading-engagement efforts and technology tools serve authentic learning goals rather than novelty or passive screen time.
formulas: Collaboration Continuum (Loertscher’s Taxonomy & Co-Teaching): move beyond simple resource gathering (coordination) to full instructional partnership—jointly setting content plus AASL standards, co-teaching inquiry/literacy mini-lessons, and co-assessing student artifacts.

UDL & Accessibility Standards: Universal Design for Learning embeds Multiple Means of Engagement, Representation, and Action & Expression; accessible library instruction supports WCAG digital standards, screen readers, alt text, captions, Bookshare/NIMAS formats, and graphic organizers.

Reading Engagement & Media Literacy: Rudine Sims Bishop’s Windows, Mirrors, and Sliding Glass Doors guides inclusive reader’s advisory; choice reading, booktalks, peer recommendations, and media-literacy deconstruction (audience, persuasion, algorithmic bias, visual framing) cultivate lifelong readers and critical media consumers.

Learning Commons & Purposeful Tech (SAMR / TPACK / ISTE): redesign library spaces into flexible zones for quiet study, collaborative creation, and makerspaces; TPACK integrates Technological, Pedagogical, and Content Knowledge while SAMR pushes tech beyond basic Substitution toward Modification and Redefinition.
decisionRules: When a 10th-grade history teacher asks at 7:45 a.m. for a cart of Civil War books for third period → fulfill the immediate need helpfully, then invite the teacher to co-plan the upcoming unit’s primary-source inquiry, database mini-lesson, and shared rubric.

When a reluctant 6th-grade reader avoids chapter novels during independent reading → conduct a brief interest-based reader’s advisory conversation and offer high-interest graphic novels, nonfiction, audiobooks, or verse novels without shaming reading level.

When selecting a new digital storytelling tool for a co-taught science unit → evaluate accessibility (captions, keyboard navigation), student data-privacy compliance (FERPA/COPPA), and TPACK/SAMR instructional value before adoption.

When students with reading disabilities struggle to synthesize long encyclopedia articles during research → pair UDL scaffolds such as read-aloud database tools, chunked note-taking organizers, and multimodal product options while maintaining inquiry rigor.
cautions: Never equate reading graphic novels, audiobooks, or nonfiction with lesser reading; multimodal and choice formats build vocabulary, fluency, and stamina.
Do not adopt flashy ed-tech apps or makerspace gadgets that collect student PII without district privacy vetting or lack alignment to learning objectives.
Avoid treating library instruction as isolated decontextualized Dewey-decimal worksheets divorced from authentic classroom curriculum.

quickReference.title: Instructional Leadership, Evidence-Based Advocacy & Community Partnerships
quickReference.purpose: Anchors job-embedded professional learning, schoolwide committee leadership, data-backed library advocacy, and external partnerships.
checklist: Align professional-learning workshops and coaching with real teacher pain points, schoolwide literacy goals, and emerging information/AI tools.
Frame library advocacy around student learning outcomes, equity, and school priorities rather than defending librarian job tasks in isolation.
Check ethics, reciprocal benefit, and sustainability when building public-library, family, and community partnerships.
formulas: Instructional Leadership & Job-Embedded PD: school librarians lead schoolwide capacity by serving on curriculum, technology, and MTSS committees, modeling copyright/AI literacy and database integration, and coaching peers inside PLCs rather than waiting passively for invitations.

Evidence-Based Advocacy Framework (AASL): effective advocacy connects library investments (certified staffing, flexible access, diverse collections) directly to stakeholder priorities—literacy growth, inquiry readiness, digital safety, and equity—using concise annual impact reports and student-work stories.

Strategic Partnerships & Outreach: formal partnerships with public libraries (reciprocal student library cards, summer reading bridges), parent organizations, local museums, and regional library consortia expand resources and family literacy beyond school hours.

Professional Ethics & Reflective Growth (ALA Code of Ethics): librarians uphold equitable service, intellectual freedom, patron privacy, and copyright integrity while growing via action research, state/national networks (AASL/ALA/ISTE), and peer mentoring.
decisionRules: When a school board considers cutting certified librarian hours to save budget funds → present a concise data-driven impact report tying co-taught units, literacy engagement, equitable device/database access, and student inquiry outcomes to district strategic goals.

When faculty express confusion and anxiety about student generative-AI use in research assignments → volunteer to lead a practical, hands-on PLC session on citation ethics, process-based inquiry prompts, and lateral verification.

When summer reading loss disproportionately affects elementary and middle-school students from lower-income households → partner with the local public library to issue student e-cards, host bilingual family literacy nights, and co-promote accessible summer borrowing.

When seeking to evaluate whether a new inquiry-scaffolding routine improved 8th-grade source quality → run a collaborative action-research cycle with an ELA teacher comparing rubric scores across semesters and share findings at a faculty meeting or state conference.
cautions: Never frame library advocacy solely around saving jobs or protecting shelves; decision-makers respond to documented impact on student learning and equity.
Do not wait passively in the library expecting teachers and administrators to discover new resources; proactive outreach and visibility build instructional partnerships.
Avoid accepting vendor sponsorships, gifts, or donated materials that compromise unbiased selection standards, student data privacy, or ALA ethical independence.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Stealth Weeding or Quiet Removal Instead of Board Reconsideration Policy
misconceptionFamilies.description: Quietly pulling, hiding behind the desk, labeling with restrictive warnings, or "stealth weeding" a controversial title in response to an informal complaint or fear of controversy instead of following the district's board-approved selection and formal reconsideration policy while keeping the material accessible during review.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Uphold intellectual freedom and the Library Bill of Rights: never censor or quietly pull challenged materials; listen respectfully, share the written board-approved reconsideration procedure, keep the item on the shelf during formal review, and document objective selection criteria.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Fixed-Coverage Scheduling Instead of Flexible Co-Taught Inquiry
misconceptionFamilies.description: Treating the school library solely as a fixed weekly rotation to cover classroom teachers' planning periods—isolating library lessons from curriculum units—rather than advocating for flexible (or blended flexible) scheduling that enables point-of-need co-planning, co-teaching, and co-assessment of inquiry.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Align library access to curriculum needs through flexible scheduling and instructional collaboration: co-design inquiry objectives with classroom teachers, embed information-literacy instruction at the exact moment students research, and co-assess student learning.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Relying on Circulation-Only Metrics Instead of Needs-Based Collection and CREW Weeding
misconceptionFamilies.description: Buying books strictly by popularity lists or judging collection quality by raw book count and circulation totals alone while ignoring collection mapping to curriculum standards, diversity audits, average publication age, and systematic CREW/MUSTIE deselection.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Base collection development and deselection on comprehensive needs assessment: map holdings to curriculum and student demographics, verify authoritative professional reviews, apply CREW/MUSTIE criteria continuously, and tie budget proposals to documented learning gaps.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Treating Educational Use as Automatic Fair Use
misconceptionFamilies.description: Advising teachers or students that nonprofit school projects automatically qualify for fair use—allowing wholesale scanning of workbooks, streaming personal consumer movie accounts for Friday reward days, or posting copyrighted images publicly without weighing the four Section 107 factors, TEACH Act limits, or open-license alternatives.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Coach faculty and students to evaluate all four fair-use factors (purpose/transformativeness, nature, amount/substantiality, and market effect), distinguish face-to-face instructional exemptions from reward entertainment, verify database/Creative Commons licenses, and model ethical attribution.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Violating Patron Circulation Privacy or Overblocking Under CIPA
misconceptionFamilies.description: Keeping permanent student checkout histories in the ILS, posting overdue lists with student names and book titles publicly, sharing a student's reading history with curious staff or non-authorized requestors, or configuring CIPA internet filters so aggressively that legitimate health, civic, and curriculum research is blocked with no prompt unblocking path.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Minimize data retention by purging circulation histories once items return, safeguard patron confidentiality under FERPA and ALA ethics, and implement CIPA filtering narrowly paired with digital-citizenship education and a fast, transparent site-unblocking protocol.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Operating as a Passive Book Warehouse Instead of AASL Instructional, UDL, and Staffing Leadership
misconceptionFamilies.description: Confining the school librarian's role to shelving, checkouts, and static CRAAP checklists while missing opportunities to lead AASL Shared Foundations inquiry, teach lateral reading against online misinformation, design UDL-accessible spaces and collections, and advocate for staffing and budgets with student-learning impact data.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Position the school library as an active instructional hub grounded in AASL Shared Foundations: teach lateral reading and verification, embed UDL physical and digital accessibility, lead faculty professional learning, and present outcome-focused evidence to administrators and boards.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Stealth Weeding or Quiet Removal Instead of Board Reconsideration Policy
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Follow Board-Approved Reconsideration Policy Instead of Stealth Weeding or Self-Censorship
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A parent, teacher, or administrator objects informally to a library book's themes and asks the librarian to quietly discard it during weeding, move it to a restricted shelf requiring permission slips, or skip buying similar titles to avoid complaints.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this response honor the written board-approved reconsideration policy and preserve open access during review, or does it commit stealth censorship, prejudicial labeling, or self-censorship?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Spot disguised censorship traps in Praxis 5312 choices: "stealth weeding" a challenged title under the pretext of shelf space, slapping age/content warning stickers on books (prejudicial labeling), locking items behind the desk, or silently removing a book before the committee meets.
stages.requiredOutput: Identify the exact intellectual-freedom violation in each distractor and distinguish objective CREW weeding from viewpoint-based removal.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Sequence the legally and ethically defensible challenge protocol: listen calmly without arguing → explain the board-approved selection policy and offer the written Request for Reconsideration form → notify the principal → keep the item circulating while a representative committee evaluates the work as a whole → abide by the formal board decision.
stages.requiredOutput: Write a 5-step formal reconsideration workflow highlighting why the material stays accessible throughout committee review.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: An angry caregiver emails demanding immediate removal of a starred-review middle-grade novel by Friday, and an assistant principal suggests "just pulling it quietly for a month until things cool down."
stages.requiredOutput: Draft the librarian's professional response to both the caregiver and the administrator grounded in board policy, ALA Library Bill of Rights principles, and documented selection reviews.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-read a fresh School Librarian 5312 item about book challenges, weeding policy disputes, or defending diverse collection acquisitions.
stages.requiredOutput: Choose the policy-anchored, transparent reconsideration or objective-selection response while rejecting unilateral removal or self-censorship.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Fixed-Coverage Scheduling Instead of Flexible Co-Taught Inquiry
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Advance Flexible Scheduling and Co-Taught Curriculum-Integrated Inquiry
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A library scheduling or teaching item depicts classes cycling through a rigid 30-minute weekly slot while classroom teachers leave for prep—leading to standalone library-skills worksheets—and a distractor accepts fixed coverage as easier to manage.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this scheduling and instructional model connect information-literacy lessons directly to authentic classroom units through co-planning, co-teaching, and co-assessment at the point of need?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Identify signs of isolated library delivery (fixed planning-coverage blocks, isolated Dewey-decimal drills, teachers dropping off classes without co-planning) versus authentic collaborative inquiry aligned to content and AASL standards.
stages.requiredOutput: Contrast the instructional impact of fixed coverage versus flexible or blended flexible scheduling on point-of-need research mastery.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Apply the full instructional-partner cycle (co-plan aligned objectives → co-teach search strategy and synthesis inside the content unit → co-assess the research process and final product) and use a phased transition (such as blended fixed-flex blocks or pilot grade-level partnerships) when a school currently runs a fixed schedule.
stages.requiredOutput: List three concrete steps a librarian can propose to a principal to transition from rigid fixed scheduling toward flexible collaborative access.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Fifth-grade teachers send students to the library only during fixed Thursday prep blocks while assigning an unrelated state-history research paper in class, resulting in copy-pasted web paragraphs. Redesign the partnership.
stages.requiredOutput: Outline a co-planned, co-taught 3-session inquiry sequence integrating state-history objectives, keyword/database search scaffolding, and a shared note-taking and citation rubric.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Evaluate a new Praxis 5312 teaching-and-learning item involving collaborative planning disagreements, standards alignment, or instructional leadership.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the option that treats the librarian as an equal instructional co-planner and co-assessor delivering point-of-need inquiry instruction.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Relying on Circulation-Only Metrics Instead of Needs-Based Collection and CREW Weeding
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Drive Collection Development and CREW Weeding Through Needs Assessment and Curriculum Mapping
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A collection-management vignette shows a librarian refusing to weed outdated 1998 astronomy or medical books to keep volume counts high, or allocating the entire budget to bestselling fiction based solely on raw circulation counts.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Are acquisitions and deselection guided by curriculum mapping, demographic/diversity needs assessment, authoritative reviews, and CREW/MUSTIE criteria—not raw circulation totals or shelf-count inflation?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Spot collection-management traps: hoarding inaccurate or shabby books to inflate books-per-student ratios, relying solely on circulation counts while ignoring non-circulating curriculum gaps, or buying unreviewed donations and vendor bundles without aligning to selection policy.
stages.requiredOutput: Flag which metric is misleading in the stem and name the missing collection-analysis evidence (curriculum map, average copyright age, diversity audit, or MUSTIE trigger).

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Operationalize the CREW method and MUSTIE criteria (Misleading/factually inaccurate, Ugly/worn, Superseded by new edition, Trivial, Irrelevant to community/curriculum, Elsewhere readily available) alongside a continuous needs-assessment cycle linking curriculum changes and learner demographics directly to budget priorities.
stages.requiredOutput: Write a concise MUSTIE decision check and explain why pruning outdated nonfiction typically increases overall library circulation and trust.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: A library audit reveals an average 500s/600s science copyright year of 2004, strong graphic-novel circulation, zero dual-language nonfiction for a growing 22% multilingual population, and a principal asking for a zero-based budget rationale.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify which holdings to weed using MUSTIE, which selection tools to consult for replacement titles, and how to tie the budget request directly to curriculum standards and learner needs.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Solve a fresh Praxis 5312 program-administration or organization-access scenario on collection development, cataloging discoverability, budget stewardship, or weeding disputes.
stages.requiredOutput: Choose the evidence-based, curriculum-mapped, CREW-aligned collection decision over raw circulation or shelf-filling habits.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Treating Educational Use as Automatic Fair Use
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Apply Four-Factor Fair Use, Licensing Terms, and Ethical Attribution Across the School
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A teacher or student asks whether a school can show a commercial streaming movie as an attendance reward, post scanned textbook chapters on a public website, or reuse copyrighted photographs in a published student podcast "because it is for education."
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this proposed use pass a balanced four-factor Section 107 fair-use analysis (or specific face-to-face/TEACH Act exemption and license terms), or is the option mistakenly assuming nonprofit schooling grants blanket immunity?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Identify copyright misconceptions in the stem: equating nonprofit education with automatic fair use, confusing face-to-face instructional movie clips (Section 110(1)) with entertainment reward screenings (which require a public performance license), or overlooking contract terms in streaming and database licenses.
stages.requiredOutput: Name the specific copyright misconception and identify which of the four fair-use factors (purpose, nature, amount, market effect) cuts against the proposed use.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Teach the practical school-librarian copyright workflow: weigh all four Section 107 factors (emphasizing transformative educational purpose and zero market harm) → check existing library database permissions and Creative Commons/public-domain sources → distinguish classroom teaching from public web distribution or reward events → model complete ethical citation.
stages.requiredOutput: Create a 4-factor fair-use check plus one clear rule distinguishing a curriculum-tied classroom film clip from an after-school or reward movie screening.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: A middle-school club wants to stream a recent commercial animated film from a teacher's personal subscription as a Friday PBIS reward, while a ninth-grade class wants to publish an open podcast using full copyrighted pop songs as background music.
stages.requiredOutput: Explain why neither use qualifies as fair use or Section 110(1) classroom exemption, and recommend the exact legal alternative (public performance license and Creative Commons/royalty-free audio with attribution) for each.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Evaluate a fresh Praxis 5312 item addressing intellectual property, digital citizenship, source attribution, or advising faculty on copyrighted instructional media.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the ethically sound, four-factor-informed guidance that equips teachers and students with lawful alternatives rather than blanket bans or blanket exemptions.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Violating Patron Circulation Privacy or Overblocking Under CIPA
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Protect Patron Circulation Confidentiality and Prevent CIPA Overblocking
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A scenario involves storing multi-year student checkout logs in the library catalog, emailing a homeroom teacher a list of specific book titles a student borrowed, or an E-rate CIPA web filter blocking reputable medical, LGBTQ+, or historical databases without an unblocking workflow.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this policy minimize identifiable patron record retention under FERPA and ALA privacy ethics while calibrating CIPA filtering narrowly with prompt access restoration for legitimate research?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Spot dual access-and-privacy traps: retaining unnecessary circulation history or exposing borrowing records publicly (violating patron confidentiality and FERPA) and equating CIPA compliance with sweeping keyword blocks that chill legitimate inquiry.
stages.requiredOutput: Flag whether the scenario's primary failure is a patron-privacy leak or CIPA overblocking, and eliminate distractors that ignore either legal duty.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Apply the two professional standards cleanly: (1) Privacy—configure the ILS to sever patron-item links automatically upon return, use private overdue notices without public title shaming, and follow board/legal procedures for any record request; (2) CIPA—block only statutory visual categories required for E-rate, pair filtering with digital-citizenship instruction, and maintain a rapid, transparent review/unblocking request process with IT.
stages.requiredOutput: Write two actionable policy safeguards: one for ILS circulation-data minimization and one for preventing and promptly resolving CIPA overblocking.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: A school's web filter blocks breast-cancer biology articles during a tenth-grade health project, and the library's ILS keeps every student's complete 4-year checkout log visible to student aides at the circulation desk.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify the immediate IT-collaboration and unblocking protocol for the health research sites and the exact ILS privacy and student-aide permission fixes.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Answer a fresh Praxis 5312 information-access or organization-access question involving ILS configuration, confidential patron records, equitable internet access, or intellectual freedom.
stages.requiredOutput: Choose the move that safeguards confidential patron records and preserves equitable, narrowly filtered access to curriculum and personal-inquiry resources.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Operating as a Passive Book Warehouse Instead of AASL Instructional, UDL, and Staffing Leadership
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Lead with AASL Shared Foundations, Lateral Reading, UDL Access, and Evidence-Based Advocacy
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: A leadership or information-literacy vignette shows a librarian staying behind the circulation desk, teaching outdated surface-level URL checks ("trust .org sites"), ignoring physical/digital accessibility barriers, or defending library funding with anecdotes instead of student-learning impact data.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does the librarian actively lead AASL inquiry, lateral-reading verification, UDL-accessible design, and outcome-driven advocacy—rather than functioning as a passive book custodian?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Spot passive-custodian and outdated-literacy distractors: relying on ".edu/.org" domain heuristics instead of lateral reading, retrofitting accessibility only after a complaint instead of proactive UDL, or arguing for staffing using book-shelving volume rather than instructional impact.
stages.requiredOutput: Identify which active leadership pillar (AASL Shared Foundations, lateral reading, UDL accessibility, or evidence-based advocacy) the stem tests.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Integrate four modern school-librarian leadership practices: align lessons to AASL Shared Foundations (Inquire, Include, Collaborate, Curate, Explore, Engage); teach SIFT lateral reading (leave the site to verify the source and claims); apply UDL across physical signage, shelf height, audiobooks, and WCAG-accessible databases; and report co-taught learning outcomes and equity metrics to principals and boards.
stages.requiredOutput: Write one crisp example of teaching lateral reading (replacing ".org" trust) and one outcome-based metric stronger than checkout count for advocating library staffing.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Facing a proposed 0.5 FTE staffing cut, a high school librarian also notices eleventh-graders citing a polished advocacy blog with a ".org" domain as an unbiased scientific source and students with visual/reading disabilities struggling to navigate print-only displays.
stages.requiredOutput: Propose an integrated plan covering a co-taught SIFT lateral-reading mini-lesson, two UDL physical/digital accessibility upgrades, and an evidence-based advocacy brief linking co-taught inquiry gains to certified librarian staffing.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Evaluate a fresh Praxis 5312 item on source evaluation, differentiation and accessibility, faculty professional learning, or stakeholder advocacy.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the proactive, AASL-aligned, UDL-accessible, evidence-driven leadership choice while rejecting passive warehouse or surface-checklist distractors.
